chapters.title: Tithing: What the Torah Asked and How Jews Practised It
chapters.subtitle: A tenth of the harvest for Levites, feasts and the poor, and what that means for Christian giving
chapters.nutshell: The Torah's tithes were a tenth of the harvest and the flocks of the land of Israel, not of money income. They fed the Levites and priests, paid for joyful family feasts in Jerusalem, and supported the poor. Later Judaism turned this into charity from income (*tzedakah*), and the New Testament calls Christians to generous, cheerful, voluntary giving.
chapters.bigIdea: The biblical tithe was a pattern of worship, joy and justice built on the harvest, and its heart, generosity to God and the poor, still stands.
skeleton: Abraham and Jacob gave a tenth before the Law
The Torah's tithes: produce and flocks, for Levites, feasts and the poor
Later Jewish giving: tzedakah and Maimonides' ladder
The New Testament: generous, cheerful, voluntary giving

p: The Hebrew word for tithe is *ma'aser*, from *eser*, “ten”. Deuteronomy 14:22 doubles the verb for emphasis: *aser te'aser*, “you shall surely tithe”. Later rabbis played on the sound: *aser bishvil she-tit'asher*, “tithe so that you will become rich” (Talmud Ta'anit 9a), because *ashar*, “to be rich”, sounds almost the same. That is a later wordplay, not the plain meaning of the verse.

Abraham gave Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, a tenth of the spoils after a battle (Gen 14:20). It was a single gift, and he gave the rest away (14:23–24). Jacob vowed at Bethel, “of all that you give me I will give a full tenth to you”, on condition that God brought him home safely (Gen 28:20–22). Tithes to temples and kings were common in the ancient Near East; Samuel warned that a king “will take the tenth of your grain… and of your flocks” (1 Sam 8:15, 17).

sections.h: Produce, not pay: the Torah's tithes
p: The Torah tithed what grew and what was born: grain, new wine, oil and fruit, and every tenth animal that “passes under the shepherd's rod” (Lev 27:30–33). The Levites had no land, so they received the tithe as their share (Num 18:21–24), and they gave a tenth of it to the priests (Num 18:26–28).

Deuteronomy adds a tithe eaten by the family itself in Jerusalem: “eat it before the LORD… and rejoice, you and your household”. If the journey was too far, it could be turned into money and spent on “whatever you desire: oxen or sheep or wine or strong drink” (Deut 14:22–27). Every third year the tithe was stored in the towns for “the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow” (Deut 14:28–29; 26:12–15). The rabbis read these as three different tithes; others think Deuteronomy reshaped one tithe. Estimates of the total, perhaps 20–23% in some years, vary.

After the exile the people promised to bring tithes to “the storerooms of the house of our God” (Neh 10:37–39). When the tithes stopped, the Levites left the Temple to farm their own fields (Neh 13:10–12). This is the setting of Malachi 3:8–12: “Bring the full tithe into the storehouse.” It is spoken to the whole nation and its priests within the covenant; the storehouse is the Temple's storeroom, and the curse is the covenant sanction of Deuteronomy 28 on a land whose harvests fail. God's promise to “open the windows of heaven” is about rain and crops in that land.

sections.h: Jesus, the Pharisees and later Jewish giving
p: The Pharisees tithed even mint, dill and cumin. Jesus said, “these you ought to have done, without neglecting the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness” (Matt 23:23). In his parable a Pharisee boasts, “I give tithes of all that I get” (Luke 18:12). The Mishnah later regulates *demai*, produce that might not have been tithed.

After the Temple fell in AD 70, tithing of produce lapsed in practice, especially outside the Land. Later Judaism developed *ma'aser kesafim*, giving a tenth of money income to charity; scholars and rabbis debate whether it is a biblical duty or a rabbinic custom. The Talmud records a ruling from Usha that one should not give more than a fifth, so that the giver does not become poor (Ketubot 50a). The great word became *tzedakah*: righteousness and justice, shown as charity. Maimonides (12th century) set out eight levels of giving; later homes kept a *pushke*, a little charity box.

sections.h: The New Testament and Christian giving
p: The New Testament never commands believers to tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular and proportionate (“as he may prosper”, 1 Cor 16:2), generous and cheerful: “not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor 9:7). Paul's great collection was for the poor in Jerusalem (2 Cor 8–9). Jesus praised the widow who gave two small coins, “all she had to live on” (Mark 12:41–44), and the first believers shared so that “there was not a needy person among them” (Acts 2:44–45; 4:32–35). Hebrews 7 mentions Abraham's tithe only to show that Melchizedek is greater than Levi.

Christians differ. Many churches teach a tenth of income as a helpful starting standard for giving. Others see the tithe as part of the Old Covenant and stress free, grace-shaped generosity. Both sides agree that giving should be generous, joyful and caring for the poor, and that it is never a way to buy God's favour.

keyPoints: *Ma'aser* means “a tenth”; the Torah's tithes were of crops and flocks in the land of Israel, not money income.
The tithes fed the landless Levites and priests, paid for joyful family feasts in Jerusalem and supported the poor.
Malachi 3 speaks to the post-exilic nation and its Temple storehouse within the covenant.
After AD 70, Judaism turned toward *tzedakah* and a later custom of giving a tenth of income, with a limit of a fifth.
The New Testament calls for generous, proportionate, cheerful and voluntary giving, especially for the poor.

chapters.title: Wealth and Prosperity: a Jewish and Biblical View
chapters.subtitle: Wealth as gift, danger and responsibility, and a fair look at the modern prosperity gospel
chapters.nutshell: The Bible calls wealth a gift of God and a blessing, but also a danger that makes people forget him. The Torah binds wealth to obligations toward the poor, the prophets condemn luxury built on injustice, and Jesus warns that no one can serve God and money. The modern prosperity gospel rightly says God cares about daily life, but departs from Scripture when it promises wealth as a reward for faith and giving.
chapters.bigIdea: In the Bible, true prosperity is shalom with God and neighbour, and wealth is a trust to be shared, not proof of God's favour.
skeleton: Wealth is a gift and a danger
Hebrew words: shalom, tsalach, osher, kavod, chayil
God's economy: the land is his, and the poor have a share
The Bible's own debate: Job, Psalm 73, Ecclesiastes
Jesus and the apostles on money
The modern prosperity gospel: a fair look

p: Abraham, Job and Solomon were rich, and the Bible counts their wealth as God's blessing. “It is he who gives you power to get wealth, that he may confirm his covenant” (Deut 8:18). But the verse before warns against saying, “My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth” (Deut 8:17). Agur prays, “give me neither poverty nor riches… lest I be full and deny you, or be poor and steal” (Prov 30:8–9), and “better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it” (Prov 15:16).

*Shalom* is wholeness: health, peace, right relationships and enough, not just money. *Tsalach* means to succeed or go well; Joshua and the righteous of Psalm 1 “prosper” by doing God's will (Josh 1:8; Ps 1:3). *Osher* is riches. *Kavod* means weight and glory, and also wealth: Abram was “very heavy” in livestock, silver and gold (Gen 13:2). *Chayil* is strength, valour and wealth; the *eshet chayil* of Proverbs 31:10 is a woman of strength and worth.

In the Torah wealth comes with duties. Farmers left the edges of fields and the gleanings for the poor and the stranger (Lev 19:9–10), which is how Ruth fed Naomi (Ruth 2). The poor tithe fed the needy. Every seventh year debts were released (Deut 15), and in the Jubilee land returned to its families, because “the land is mine; you are strangers and sojourners with me” (Lev 25:23).

The prophets attacked wealth built on injustice: the “cows of Bashan” who crush the needy (Amos 4:1), those who lounge on ivory beds while ignoring ruin (Amos 6:4–6), and those who “join house to house” and seize fields (Isa 5:8; Mic 2:2).

Job's friends argued that the righteous prosper and the suffering must have sinned. God said they had not spoken rightly (Job 42:7). Psalm 73 wrestles with “the prosperity of the wicked” until the psalmist sees their end in God's sanctuary. Ecclesiastes calls the love of wealth “vanity” and praises enjoying God's gifts with contentment (Eccl 5:10–20). Later, the Mishnah asks, “Who is rich? One who rejoices in his portion” (Avot 4:1). Jewish teaching also praises the “good eye”, a generous heart (Prov 22:9).

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles on money
p: Jesus said, “You cannot serve God and money” (Matt 6:24); “mammon” is probably the Aramaic *mamona*, wealth. The rich young ruler went away sad, and Jesus said it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom (Mark 10:17–27). The idea of a small “Needle Gate” in Jerusalem is a late story with no ancient support. He told of the rich fool (Luke 12:13–21) and of Lazarus and the rich man (Luke 16:19–31), and he welcomed Zacchaeus, who gave half his goods to the poor (Luke 19:1–10).

Paul wrote, “godliness with contentment is great gain… the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils”, and told the rich to be “rich in good works” (1 Tim 6:6–10, 17–19). James warned rich oppressors (Jas 5:1–6; 2:1–7). “I can do all things” (Phil 4:13) is about contentment in hunger and plenty, not a promise of success. In 3 John 2, “I pray that you may prosper and be in health” uses a standard ancient letter greeting, “that all may go well with you”.

sections.h: The prosperity gospel: a fair look
p: The prosperity gospel is a modern movement, not one church. A common historical account traces it to 19th- and 20th-century American currents: New Thought ideas about the power of the mind, “positive confession”, healing revivals and post-war affluence. Its core claims are that faith and giving bring guaranteed health and wealth, that a gift is a “seed” God will multiply, and that speaking words of faith brings them about. It has spread widely across Africa, Asia and Latin America.

It draws people for real reasons: hope for the poor, and the true belief that God cares about bodies, work and daily bread. But it departs from Jewish and biblical teaching when it treats wealth as proof of God's favour (the view of Job's friends), giving as an investment rather than justice for the poor, and suffering as a lack of faith, when Jesus called his followers to take up the cross and Paul learned contentment.

diagrams.title: Eight rich and poor people in Scripture

cards.front: Rich in flocks, silver and gold.
cards.back: God blessed Abraham with great wealth, yet he gave Melchizedek a tenth and refused to keep the king of Sodom's spoils, so no one could say a man made him rich.

cards.front: The richest man in the East, then nothing.
cards.back: Job lost everything, and his friends said it must be his sin. God rejected their view. Job worshipped: “the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away.”
cards.echo: Suffering is not proof of God's anger (John 9:2–3).

cards.front: Asked for wisdom, received wealth too.
cards.back: Solomon asked for wisdom and God added riches and honour. But his gold, horses and many wives later turned his heart away, as Deuteronomy had warned.
cards.echo: Deut 17:16–17 warns kings against piling up gold.

cards.front: A widow gleaning in a rich man's field.
cards.back: Boaz obeyed the gleaning laws and went further, letting Ruth glean among the sheaves. His generosity became redemption, and their line led to David.
cards.echo: Matthew lists Ruth in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:5).

cards.front: A handful of flour and a little oil.
cards.back: A poor foreign widow shared her last meal with Elijah, and the flour and oil did not run out through the famine.

cards.front: He kept the commandments but went away sad.
cards.back: Jesus loved him and asked him to sell all, give to the poor and follow. He left grieving, “for he had great possessions”.

cards.front: A rich tax collector climbs a tree.
cards.back: After Jesus came to his house, Zacchaeus gave half his goods to the poor and repaid fourfold anyone he had cheated. Jesus said, “Today salvation has come to this house.”
cards.echo: Repaying fourfold echoes the Torah's law of restitution (Ex 22:1).

cards.front: Two tiny coins in the Temple box.
cards.back: The rich gave large sums, but a poor widow put in two small copper coins. Jesus said she gave more than all, because she gave all she had to live on.
cards.echo: God measures the heart, not the amount (2 Cor 8:12).

keyPoints: The Bible calls wealth a gift of God and a blessing, and also a danger that can make people forget him.
*Shalom* is wholeness, not just money; to “prosper” (*tsalach*) is to succeed in doing God's will.
Torah binds wealth to the poor: gleaning, the poor tithe, the Sabbath year and the Jubilee, because the land is God's.
Job, Psalm 73 and Ecclesiastes reject the idea that wealth proves righteousness; Jesus warns that no one can serve God and money.
The prosperity gospel rightly says God cares about daily needs, but wrongly promises wealth as a reward for faith and giving.
